title: The three-minute tour
blurb: Five beats in one evening and the next afternoon: a reflex in code, a request with no wake word, a mention that is not a request, a TV that is not a resident, and a safety rule that does not wait for a model.

steps.text: Three minutes in the Zhang-Rivera home. Every sensor here is simulated; the two deciders are real models running on this machine. Watch what the house does, and what it refuses to do.
Beat 1 of 5. 23:40 on a Tuesday. Alex and Sam are on the couch with the lights off; the kitchen is pitch black. Alex gets up for a snack.
The kitchen light came on in milliseconds. A plain rule did that: dark room, a person walking in, night, lights off. No model was asked.
For comparison, the 2B scene decider needs about a second on this scene and was only 63% sure of 'turn on lights'. Reflexes stay in code.
Beat 2. Alex comes back with the snack and talks to Sam. No wake word, no command words.
I can't see a thing in here.
The keyword baseline heard no command at all. The 2B model was unsure (67% in the bench), so the 12B was asked: 'lights on'. When the house is still unsure it asks Alex's phone first.
Living room lights on, either straight away or after a 'Yes' on the phone.
Beat 3. Sam complains about work.
I left the lights on at the office again, my boss is going to kill me.
A keyword system heard 'lights on' and would have flipped a switch. The decider read the whole sentence: it is about the office, not this house. Nothing moved.
Under the hood the 2B leaned to 'lights off' at 76%, below the act threshold, so the 12B was asked and answered 'not a request'.
Beat 4. They put on a movie and dim the lights.
Turn off the lights.
The mic array heard those words from the TV's direction. The voice agent tagged the source 'tv' and the policy denied it, whatever the words meant.
A keyword system would have obeyed the movie. In the bench both models obeyed it too: who is speaking is a rule, not a model call.
Beat 5. The next afternoon, 17:20. Sam is cooking; a pot is on the stove.
The doorbell rings. Sam steps out to the living room; Maya, 7, wanders into the kitchen.
standing on a chair next to the stove, reaching for the pot
Perception flagged a hazard: a child next to a lit burner with no adult in the room. The alert is a plain rule, so it fires even when a model is unsure. The scene decider agreed anyway (2B 92%).
Sam's phone buzzes with the camera frame.
Five beats: a reflex in code, understanding without a wake word, a mention that is not a request, a TV that is not a resident, and a safety rule that does not wait for a model.
Rules where they belong; models where words and scenes need understanding.
